newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Kuwait denies buying China guns, British missiles.
newsitem.headline: Kuwait denies buying China guns, British missiles.

text.p: Kuwait said on Tuesday it had not signed any deals for the purchase of British missiles or Chinese self-propelled guns.
"As I said, no contracts have been signed," acting premier and foreign minister Sheikh Sabah al-Ahmad al-Sabah told reporters at parliament.
"The decision will come later," he said, when asked if Kuwait had decided to buy the Chinese howitzers.
Earlier on Tuesday diplomatic and industry sources said Kuwait's key Western allies were expected to press the Gulf Arab state to reverse a decision to buy the guns from China.

There has been no official announcement on the deal but the sources said a Kuwaiti military committee had recently picked the Chinese to equip a Kuwait Land Forces batallion with 18 howitzers with an option for a second batallion.
"Only one of the (Kuwaiti) officers at the committee meeting abstained while the others backed the Chinese offer," a Western industry expert told Reuters.
Western industry sources said the price for equipping one batallion with tracked howitzers was around $200 million.

Diplomatic sources said they expect William Cohen, who will make his first visit to Kuwait as U.S. Defence Secretary in mid-June, and British Foreign Office Minister Derek Fatchett, due to arrive on June 23, to raise the issue of the guns.
"You bet they (Britain and the United States) are not happy with that decision," said an industry expert. They are proposing their own weapons, saying they are superior.

In competition with China, Washington, which led the 1991 Gulf War, hopes to sell Kuwait its M109 A6 Paladin. The British are pushing hard to sell the Desert AS90. South Africa has offered its wheeled LIW 155mm G6.
Since it was freed from a seven-month Iraqi occupation, Kuwait has had a policy of awarding key weapons contracts to the five permanent members of the United Nations Security Council.

Kuwait has defence and cooperation pacts with China, Russia, France, Britain and the United States. All but China have won arms contracts since the Gulf War but Beijing has secured other lucrative state deals.
Some recent arms deals have been put on hold due to parliament's insistence on reviewing contracts.

The British minister is expected to also discuss Kuwait's apparent freezing of a decision to buy British Aerospace Plc Sea Skua missiles in a deal worth about $90 million. Some MPs want parliament to probe the deal, made after a cheaper offer by France's Aerospatiale MM-15 was dropped.
Sheikh Sabah told parliament on Tuesday "no deal has been signed concerning these missiles". Kuwait had earlier said a decision to buy Sea Skuas was final.
